easy.explanation: Verse 1 says that Eliphaz the Temanite answered.
easy.q: Who answered at the beginning of the chapter?

answers: He had instructed and strengthened others
He had seen visions in the night
easy.explanation: Eliphaz says that Job had instructed many and strengthened weak hands and feeble knees.
easy.q: What had Job done in the past according to Eliphaz?

easy.explanation: Eliphaz says, “now it is come upon thee, and thou faintest.”
easy.q: What happened to Job when trouble came upon him?

answers: To show the contrast between Job’s former strength and his present weakness
To tell the story of Job’s family
medium.explanation: Eliphaz contrasts Job’s former encouragement of others with his present distress.
medium.q: Why does Eliphaz mention Job’s former actions?

answers: People who are weak or discouraged
medium.explanation: The phrase describes people who needed strengthening and encouragement.
medium.q: What does the phrase “weak hands” mean in this passage?

answers: His fear, confidence, hope, and upright ways
medium.explanation: Eliphaz points to Job’s fear, confidence, hope, and uprightness as sources of support.
medium.q: What should have supported Job, according to Eliphaz?

answers: Someone who strengthened others should be able to strengthen himself
Someone who strengthened others must abandon them
Someone who suffered before cannot help others
challenge.explanation: Eliphaz expects Job to respond to his own trouble as he once helped others respond to theirs.
challenge.q: What connection does Eliphaz make between Job’s past and present?

answers: Job is struggling to stand even though he formerly strengthened others
challenge.explanation: Eliphaz focuses on the difference between Job’s former conduct and his present reaction to trouble.
challenge.q: What is the main point of Eliphaz’s rebuke?

challenge.explanation: The word “troubled” describes Job’s fearful and distressed condition.
challenge.q: Which word describes Job’s troubled reaction in verse 5?

paragraphs.title: The Wicked Reap Their Deeds and the Strong Collapse

easy.explanation: Eliphaz asks where the innocent perish and where the righteous are cut off, presenting them as those who do not perish.
easy.q: Who, according to Eliphaz, does not perish?

easy.explanation: Verse 8 says that those who sow wickedness reap the same.
easy.q: What do those who plow iniquity and sow wickedness reap?

easy.explanation: The passage mentions the lion, the fierce lion, young lions, and the old lion.
easy.q: Which animals appear in the comparison?

answers: People reap the results of their actions
Farming is the main subject of the chapter
medium.explanation: The image expresses a connection between a person’s deeds and their consequences.
medium.q: What is the main idea of the sowing and reaping image?

medium.explanation: In this context, “iniquity” means wrongdoing or sin.
medium.q: What does “iniquity” mean in the phrase “they that plow iniquity”?

medium.explanation: The lions’ roar and teeth are broken, and the old lion’s whelps are scattered.
medium.q: How is the strength of the lions described at the end of the passage?

answers: To show that even the very powerful are not safe from collapse
To describe a journey through the wilderness
challenge.explanation: The lions represent great strength, yet even they are broken and scattered.
challenge.q: Why does Eliphaz mention lions and young lions?

answers: Actions have no connection with consequences
The wicked reap what they do, while the righteous are not destroyed
challenge.explanation: Eliphaz presents a moral pattern in which wrongdoing brings destruction and the righteous endure.
challenge.q: What view of justice appears in Eliphaz’s words?

answers: Both are described as weak from the beginning
Both are connected with night visions
Both the power of the wicked and the physical power of lions can collapse
challenge.explanation: The passage compares the downfall of wicked people with the downfall of powerful lions.
challenge.q: What strengthens the transition from the wicked to the lions?

answers: Secretly, and his ear received a little of it
easy.explanation: Eliphaz says that a thing was secretly brought to him and that his ear received a little thereof.
easy.q: How did the message come to Eliphaz?

answers: In the middle of the day
In visions of the night, when deep sleep fell on men
easy.explanation: Eliphaz describes visions of the night when deep sleep fell upon men.
Fear and trembling came upon him and made all his bones shake.
easy.q: What did Eliphaz feel during the revelation?

medium.explanation: Eliphaz says, “Then a spirit passed before my face.”
Silence means stillness or quietness, from which Eliphaz heard a voice.
medium.q: What does the word “silence” mean in verse 16?

answers: The form or appearance of the spirit
medium.explanation: He says, “I could not discern the form thereof,” although an image was before his eyes.
medium.q: What was Eliphaz unable to discern?

answers: A secret message, a night vision, fear, a passing spirit, and a voice from silence
A voice, a lion, sleep, and a letter
Fear, an answer, a journey, and a conversation
challenge.explanation: This sequence follows the events described in verses 12–16.
challenge.q: What is the sequence of the revelation in this passage?

answers: The revelation emphasizes the message more than identifying the figure
Eliphaz was not asleep at all
The voice belonged to someone he knew
challenge.explanation: The passage emphasizes that Eliphaz heard a voice without clearly discerning the figure’s form.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from Eliphaz hearing a voice but not recognizing the form?

answers: The passing spirit and the voice heard from silence
challenge.explanation: The unseen form, passing spirit, silence, and mysterious voice create the vision’s atmosphere.
challenge.q: Which detail most emphasizes the mystery of the vision?

answers: A human can be more just than God
A human cannot be more just or pure than the Creator
A human has no relation to God
easy.explanation: The voice asks whether mortal man can be more just than God or more pure than his maker.
easy.q: What does the voice say about human beings in relation to God?

easy.explanation: People are described as dwelling in houses of clay whose foundation is in the dust.
easy.q: What are human beings compared to in this passage?

easy.explanation: The passage says that they are destroyed and perish.

answers: God puts no trust in them and charges them with folly
medium.explanation: Verse 18 says that God put no trust in his servants and charged his angels with folly.
medium.q: What is said about the angels before God?

answers: Human beings whose bodies are made of earthly material
medium.explanation: The phrase describes the frail, earthly nature of human beings.
medium.q: What does the phrase “houses of clay” refer to?

answers: Being founded in dust emphasizes human frailty and mortality
medium.explanation: The dust foundation highlights how easily human beings are crushed and perish.
medium.q: What is the connection between dust and human destiny?

challenge.explanation: The passage contrasts God’s righteousness and greatness with human frailty.
challenge.q: What is the central contrast in the passage?

answers: If even angels are not free from fault, humans are certainly limited before God
challenge.explanation: The comparison with angels emphasizes the great difference between God and all created beings.
challenge.q: What does the mention of angels teach about the message concerning human beings?

answers: Man can defeat God through wisdom
Man cannot claim moral superiority over his Creator
challenge.explanation: The question stresses human limitations and God’s superiority.
challenge.q: What does the question about whether man can be more just or pure than his Maker mean?
